beats.lead: Koalas carry a print no other non-primate has.
beats.text: They are the only non-primate mammal known to have true fingerprints, complete with the same loops and whorls found on human hands.
beats.note: Biological anthropologist Maciej Henneberg noticed it whilst working with koalas at a wildlife park near Adelaide in the mid-1990s.

beats.name: Maciej Henneberg
beats.role: a biological anthropologist at the University of Adelaide, examined koala fingertip ridges closely enough to conclude that even careful analysis under a microscope could struggle to tell them apart from a human's.

beats.lead: The similarity is close enough that Henneberg raised it with police.
beats.text: He told The Independent in 1996 that officers should at least be aware a koala print could resemble a human one.
beats.note: He was equally clear that finding one at an actual crime scene would be extremely unlikely.

beats.text: The popular version of this story, that koala prints have genuinely confused real detectives, does not check out.
beats.note: Fact-checkers have found no documented case of a koala print contaminating an investigation or a suspect being wrongly implicated. The genuine fingerprint similarity got exaggerated into a crime-solving myth.

beats.text: Koalas and humans do not get their nearly identical fingerprints from a shared ancestor who had them. Evolution appears to have built the same solution twice, in two completely unrelated animals reaching for a better grip.

beats.line: The only crime a koala print is actually guilty of is causing confusion in a lab.
